name: error
description: Errors as values.  A fallible call reports failure through `!`, `?`, or an `if`/`switch` arm, and the message and code it failed with live in a channel the arm reads with the `err` builtin. That channel hands back two loose values and empties itself as it is read, so what a program gets is a pair it cannot keep together: an error cannot be stored, returned, collected, or given context on the way past. `Error` is that pair as one ordinary value.  Read it first in the failure arm. `err` empties the channel, and the next fallible call clears it, so `error::last` has to run before anything else that can fail.  This module is a thin layer over the channel, not a replacement for it: raising is still `panic`, and a call site still says `!`, `?`, or reads the result with `if` or `switch`.  @example use error  fn parse_port(s:str -- port:i64)! {     s "" == if { "port is empty" 1 panic }     8080 }  fn main() {     "" parse_port if {         print nl     } else {         error::last -> e         e <<message print nl     } } doccheck: page-context doccheck: page-setup "disk full" 5 error::new -> e

structs.name: Error
structs.description: A failure: the code an `if` or `switch` arm matched on, the message `panic` was given, and the error this one was wrapped around, if there is one.  Fields:   code    - the code passed to `panic`; 0 when nothing has failed   message - the message passed to `panic`, with any wrapping context already composed in   cause   - the error this one wrapped, or null

functions.name: last
functions.description: The error the last fallible call failed with, as one value.  Reading empties the channel, so call this once, first, in the failure arm. With nothing to report it answers with code 0 and an empty message.

functions.name: new
functions.description: Build an error without raising one, for a function that returns a failure as a value.

functions.name: root
functions.description: The error at the bottom of the cause chain -- the one that actually failed.

returns.name: r
returns.description: The root cause, or the error itself when it wrapped nothing

functions.name: wrap
functions.description: Wrap an error in context from the frame that caught it.  The wrapped error keeps the original's code, so a caller matching on it in a `switch` still matches; the message reads "context: original"; and `cause` holds the error wrapped. Re-raise the result with `panic`, which the compiler reads as diverging, so the arm needs nothing after it: `e <<message e <<code panic`.
examples: e "cannot save the document" error::wrap -> wrapped
